#1022. How the US mid-term elections could shake up science

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

The upcoming US mid-term elections could change which political party controls Congress, which meets in the US Capitol building in Washington DC.Credit: Finn Gomez/Getty

As tens of millions of voters head to the polls on 3 November to cast ballots in the US mid-term elections, a political shake-up could be coming to Washington DC — with substantial consequences for the country’s scientific landscape.

Republicans currently hold more seats than do Democrats in both chambers of the US Congress, which has given the party and administration of President Donald Trump unified control of the federal government. But polling data favour Democrats to win back the House of Representatives and suggest that they have a chance of taking control of the Senate, too.

Since Trump took office last year, his administration has terminated thousands of research grants, slashed the federal scientific workforce and sought unprecedented political oversight of science agencies such as the US National Institutes of Health (NIH) and the US National Science Foundation (NSF). Many researchers and science advocates hope that a new Congress will stand up to the Trump administration to protect science funding and investigate its actions. “The Republican Congress has basically ceded their role in oversight for the last almost two years,” says Shaughnessy Naughton, president of 314 Action, a political fundraising group in Washington DC, which recruits and backs Democratic scientists, engineers and health-care specialists running for office.

The Trump administration has requested deep cuts to federal science budgets for the past couple of years, asking for the NSF’s budget, for example, to be cut by more than 50% in fiscal years 2026 and 2027. Both Republican and Democratic members of Congress, which sets the federal budget, have staved off those cuts so far. But the budget for the 2027 fiscal year, which began on 1 October, has not yet been officially approved.

White House proposes vast overhaul of US science funding: what you need to know

White House proposes vast overhaul of US science funding: what you need to know

Even if Democrats, who have been backing boosts in science spending, were to win control of both chambers of Congress, it could be difficult to push through any major funding increases, because the final budget bills must still be signed by Trump.

At a minimum, researchers and science advocates hope that Congress will continue to prevent big budget cuts. But keeping budgets steady on paper has not stopped the administration from squeezing research in practice. Without congressional approval, the White House has curbed spending in other ways — terminating active grants mid-cycle and refusing to distribute money that Congress had already approved, a controversial tactic known as impoundment.

Science advocates say they hope that a new Congress will assert its budgetary power, namely by pushing back on these actions. The NSF, for instance, closed the 2026 fiscal year on 30 September with some US$1.4 billion in unspent funds, leading to the lowest number of new research grants issued in decades. The agency said that it has two years by law to spend its approved budget.

The Government Accountability Office (GAO), the investigative arm of Congress that has the ability to determine whether funds have been impounded, has rarely pursued action over violations, says Matt Dull, a specialist in government oversight at Virginia Tech, in Blacksburg, but the mid-terms could change the situation.

Controversial White House plan to overhaul US science funding faces Senate opposition

Controversial White House plan to overhaul US science funding faces Senate opposition

Another way that Congress could push back against the Trump administration’s reshaping of US science is to attach specific conditions to funding bills. For instance, because lawmakers haven’t yet agreed on the final budget for the 2027 fiscal year, they passed a ‘stopgap’ bill that funds the government only up to 11 December. The bill contains a section that temporarily blocks a White House plan to overhaul US science.

That plan is controversial: it would, for instance, put political appointees in charge of federal grant review and allow them to override the decisions of scientist peer reviewers. Giving control of grants to political appointees would threaten biomedical progress globally, says Ellie Dehoney, senior vice-president of policy and advocacy at Research!America, a non-profit organization in Arlington, Virginia. The White House Office of Management and Budget (OMB), which created the plan, said it did so to improve transparency, accountability and oversight of federal funds.

Rosa DeLauro, a Democratic representative from Connecticut, issued a statement last month saying that she was confident that Congress would continue blocking the OMB plan in future spending bills.

Although Congress does not run US science agencies, it has oversight powers, which include launching investigations into agency actions. Most of these powers are reserved for the party in control of Congress, and Democrats have pledged to use them if they win big in the mid-terms.

‘Science needs defending’: record number of researchers run for office in US mid-terms

‘Science needs defending’: record number of researchers run for office in US mid-terms

“We will continue the work we have been doing over the past two years to hold the Trump administration accountable,” says Zoe Lofgren, the most senior Democrat on the House Science, Space and Technology (SST) Committee. “If we win, we’ll have more tools at our disposal to do exactly that.” Lofgren and her Democratic colleagues have sent numerous letters to agencies such as the NSF and the US Department of Energy asking about actions such as grant terminations but have received few answers. If Democrats take control, Lofgren, who represents a California district and could become head of the SST committee, would have the ability to issue subpoenas, which can be used to compel administrators to testify in front of Congress.

#1021. Anthony Gordon makes vow to Javier Aguirre after viral World Cup interaction

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Aguirre shouted Gordon’s name before saying ‘f*** you’ and laughing during England’s last-16 win over Mexico

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Anthony Gordon says he will sign an image of his viral interaction with Javier Aguirre from the World Cup following a request from the former Mexico manager.

Television cameras captured the moment during the first-half hydration break of England’s last-16 triumph at the Estadio Azteca, with Aguirre seen shouting Gordon’s name to get his attention before saying “f*** you” and laughing.

The clip was widely shared across social media and has been recalled as a “random moment of silliness” by Aguirre.

The 67-year-old, who like Barcelona’s Gordon made a move to LaLiga in the summer, said following his appointment as Valencia manager that he wanted the Englishman to sign a print-out of the moment for his children.

“I think that was a great interaction,” Gordon said, speaking ahead of Barcelona’s meeting with Aston Villa in the Champions League.

“People really liked it, it went viral. It was really fun, no malice and just a joke in the moment. What made it better is that there was so much pressure, tension, animosity within the game and then to make this joke in the side like we’re playing in the park.

“It was a really funny moment. He seems like a really good guy.”

Responding to Aguirre’s request for a signed photo, he responded: “I’ll sign whatever he likes!”

Gordon hailed the 3-2 win in Mexico City as “the best of my life”, which saw Thomas Tuchel’s side grit through against the World Cup co-hosts on enemy soil.

“We heard so much noise about the altitude, the stadium, the atmosphere,” he added. “It is still the loudest noise I think I’ve ever heard when they sang their national anthem.

“This will stick with me forever and the way we won, with 10 men. How we won the penalty with 10 men. There was so much emotion involved and this will live with me forever.”

Now fighting for titles at Barcelona, former Newcastle and Everton winger Gordon is thriving under the pressure of playing on the biggest stage, so far scoring three goals and grabbing four assists across 13 appearances.

He insists the expectation of winning trophies in Spain is easier to handle than the pressure of battling relegation, which he experienced while at the Toffees.

“The challenge of joining Barcelona is different to what I’ve had before because I was fighting relegation for two or three years at Everton, which was tough,” Gordon said.

“At Newcastle, we were fighting for maybe Champions League and to push up the table, and now I’m fighting with Barca for every trophy.

“So I’ve had three very different challenges as far as the teams that I played for.

“I really enjoyed all three because they come with different things to help you as a person, help you grow.

“I think to be competing on every front for every trophy, is definitely the most enjoyable. People think it’s more pressure, but it’s actually better pressure than the fight for relegation.”

The former Arsenal and Manchester United rivals are now pals off the pitch

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

As players, Ian Wright and Roy Keane spent much of their careers on opposite sides of one of English football’s fiercest rivalries.

The Arsenal great and former Manchester United captain both possessed the competitive spirit that meant exchanging pleasantries and forging friendships was never high on their to-do list when league titles were on the line.

Football, though, has that habit of bringing together different characters and the pair have now developed a genuine bond away from the pitch. This is clear to anyone who watches The Overlap, where the two rivals have had a chance to show off a different side to their personalities.

““I remember when Gary first got in touch and said who he was going to get involved,” Wright tells FourFourTwo when asked about how his link-up with Gary Neville on The Overlap came about.

“I said ‘If you could get that crew together, that’d be brilliant’. We met up, and when we spoke, it just felt natural. The way we speak on camera is the way we are with each other off camera, too.

"I’m with people I genuinely like, and we’ve got a friendship and a bond now that is real. Nobody is afraid to pull anyone else up if they get something wrong or say something we don’t agree with, but it’s everyone’s love for the game that really comes across.”

During Wright and Keane's pomp in the 1990s, Arsenal and Manchester United's title battles set up a number of era-defining bitter Premier League clashes, making it hard for anyone to believe that two of the main protagonists would end up as such good friends.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

“Mine and Roy’s relationship on the pitch was fractious,” Wright admits. “If I came in his vicinity, it was never going to be nice.

“But that was because of the teams we were playing for and what was expected of us, especially trying to deal with that Man United side. It was so dominant and so great.

"If you’d said to me back then that we would be friends now, would I have believed it? No, never. I never would have thought we’d be this close."

However, as the duo embarked on successful media careers, they soon found that they were kindred spirits.

“But it started when we were both doing punditry," former England man Wright adds. "We met up a few times and it was just fine, because people don’t understand Roy, he’s not an ogre! He’s not some guy that’s just in your face.

"He’ll respect you if you’re respectful, you’d never go into a studio with Roy and find he’d be rude or disrespectful. I love the fact you never know what he might say.”

For more than a decade, Joe Mewis has worked in football journalism as a reporter and editor. Mewis has had stints at Mirror Football and LeedsLive among others and worked at FourFourTwo throughout Euro 2024, reporting on the tournament. In addition to his journalist work, Mewis is also the author of four football history books that include times on Leeds United and the England national team. Now working as a digital marketing coordinator at Harrogate Town, too, Mewis counts some of his best career moments as being in the iconic Spygate press conference under Marcelo Bielsa and seeing his beloved Leeds lift the Championship trophy during lockdown.

#1018. Ousmane Dembélé quietly becomes the main man after long journey to the top

The Frenchman, who has been named the best male footballer in the world by the Guardian, has benefitted from PSG’s focus on the team rather than individuals

What makes a good player great, and a great player the best? This question has been occupying me since 2014, when the Guardian first asked me to contribute to its inaugural Next Generation feature. My job was to look for a France-based talent born in 1997 who could go on to have a stellar career.

After a great deal of research, I narrowed it down from my shortlist of five by asking questions not about the players’ football ability, but about other attributes: resilience, adaptability, decision-making, creativity, work ethic, response to feedback and willingness to learn. Qualities we cannot see, and are harder to measure.

Based on those answers, one player stood out above all the others: a kid called Ousmane Dembélé, then a youth player yet to make a first-team appearance at Rennes. Eleven years after appearing in these pages as one to watch, Dembélé has been voted the best male player in the world by the Guardian’s 219-strong voting panel.

Those intangible qualities were in full effect on the night Dembélé made good on his years of promise. The defining image of Paris Saint-Germain’s 5-0 win over Inter in the 2025 Champions League final was not the trophy lift, or any one of the goal celebrations, but Dembélé, poised on the edge of the opposition penalty area, with hunched demeanour and furrowed brow, his face a picture of focus, ready to press. Just how did he get to this point?

One lesson to learn from the Dembélé story: the path to greatness is not always linear. He started off like a train, winning France’s young player of the year award in his first season as a professional. The following season, he helped Borussia Dortmund win the German Cup.

Around that time, in the course of research for my book, Edge, I spoke to Thomas Tuchel, his coach at Dortmund. Tuchel told me that Dembélé’s talent came with an obligation and responsibility to improve. He bracketed his players into one of three “ABC” categories, depending on their dominant motivation, and would change his man-management style accordingly.

The A category stood for “aggressive-motivated”, and referred to players motivated by individual glory and awards (in Tuchel’s eyes, this was not necessarily a negative: think Neymar at Paris).

B stood for “binding-motivated”, those players who love being part of the group and bringing people together (often captains, such as César Azpilicueta at Chelsea).

C stood for “curious-motivated”. These were the players capable of greatness, who needed to be trained in a slightly different way. Their talent could take them far; and on a good day, they were capable of anything. Tuchel loved coaching these players. Dembélé, he felt, was a C.

But the journey was not always smooth. In 2017, he moved to Barcelona, who were flush with money from selling Neymar for €222m (£194m). It was a sliding doors moment. That same summer, Barcelona changed coach: in came Ernesto Valverde; out went Luis Enrique. In six injury-laden years at Barcelona, Dembélé started only a third of the league games. He scored a total of 24 league goals. His most memorable moment might have been missing a last-minute one-on-one in the 2019 Champions League semi-final against Liverpool, when Barcelona were already 3-0 up (remember what happened next? They lost the second leg 4-0). When he did leave, amid mutterings of wasted talent and blackmail, it felt like a relief for all parties.

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

There is some symmetry to Dembélé’s exceptional 2025. Of the 30 goals he has scored this calendar year at the time of writing, the most decisive and emblematic was probably against Liverpool in the second leg of their Champions League last-16 tie. With PSG 1-0 down from the first leg, Dembélé drifted into his own half, losing his markers who didn’t want to follow him that far. He picked up the ball and spread it wide to the right-winger Bradley Barcola, then sprinted into the box and made it to the cross to score. (He also scored a penalty in PSG’s successful shootout after they won 1-0 at Anfield that night). Dembélé did something similar against Arsenal in the semi-final, dropping deep early in the game, switching the play to the left-sided Khvicha Kvaratskhelia and receiving the return ball, unmarked, on the edge of the area, before scoring. Even when teams knew it was coming, they couldn’t stop him.

At the start of last season, Luis Enrique’s plan was for the whole team to replace the goals of Kylian Mbappé, who had joined Real Madrid. After all, Dembélé had not scored more than 10 league goals in a season since his debut campaign at Rennes. Luis Enrique wanted the team to be the star. And so, with no star player to serve, Dembélé was liberated. This curious-motivated talent who once scored penalties with either foot, and even took corners with either foot, quietly became the main man. He starts the press; his vision, movement, pace, control and positioning set the tone; and his finishing, once considered wasteful, is ruthless.

I still don’t know exactly what makes a good player great but I am closer to an answer. Part of the equation remains what we cannot see: the chemistry within a team, the relationship with a specific coach, playing in a system that brings out the best in every player. But also those other qualities that Dembélé had at 17, and still has now. This well-deserved prize is as much for those attributes as it is for his goals and the trophies he helped Paris Saint-Germain win.

#1017. FIFPRO report highlights growing pains in women's football

Expected global revenue of over $1 billion and new faces at the U17 World Cup show women's football is booming, but a recent report also highlights need for better structures globally.

At first glance, women's football is healthier than ever. A recent report by FIFPRO, football's global players' union, said worldwide revenue is expected to reach over $1bn (€894m) in 2027. The World Cup in Brazil, a first in South America, will be the last with 32 teams and is expected to be the most watched and biggest revenue-generating women's tournament ever.

The good news continues with the U17 Women's World Cup in Morocco, where the tournament is being held every year for five straight years. Germany, France, Spain, Brazil, the United States and defending champions North Korea are all at the 2026 edition of a competition whose reputation continues to grow.

"You can just see where the game is going, which is so exciting," US head coach Ciara Crinion told FIFA. "The level has just gone up. We have to continue to stay with that and compete as well. [The U-17 Women's World Cup] almost feels like that first stepping stone in a major tournament for young players, and now you see how serious it is taken."

Puerto Rico, Australia and Argentina are making their debuts. For Puerto Rico, qualification is historic, as no football team in the men's or women's game has ever reached a World Cup tournament before.

"We've embraced this idea of being Puerto Rico's first team to qualify for a World Cup," head coach Andres Mirabelli told FIFA. Alongside national development plans, player recruitment was aided by a diaspora of nearly four million in the United States, perhaps the strongest place for women's football in the world. According to FIFPRO, the regional football average salary in North America is $5,940 (€5,547) per month, which is far higher than any other continent.

But even for the handful of players who make it out of these youth tournaments to a professional career, creating a living out of the beautiful game remains a real challenge. The aforementioned FIFPRO report details that many professional female players across the world barely earn minimum wage, with some even falling below it.

The report, which sourced its data from player surveys across the world, found that only 66% of professional players are paid for 12 months a year. The global average salary is $2,600 (€2,300) a month, but the range varies drastically across the world. In Eastern Europe, for example, that average is $880 per month. In Africa, it is $432, but in North America it is just under $6,000.

"I think what you also find in the women's game is the gaps are not just between the top five leagues and the rest. There is a gap there, but even within leagues themselves [there is one]," FIFPRO head of research and strategy for women's football Frankie Brown told DW.

"In some of the other leagues you're dealing with teams that are operating professionally, so will be paying their players on a reasonable wage, and playing in the same league as them you'll have players that are on amateur contracts and not being paid at all."

With economic and job security an issue for many, the report reveals that psychological stress factors are now the second main reason many consider leaving football.

"This is one of the most concerning parts of the report," Alex Culvin, the director of women's football at FIFPRO, said in a statement.

"Of the 49% of women’s football players considering leaving the sport early, 46% cited their mental health as the reason. In interviews, players say the sport's growth brings new pressures — including extra workload and social media abuse — but that clubs do not have the necessary safeguards in place to support these changes. We want clubs and national associations to provide mandatory mental health support focused on wellbeing, which is independent of sporting performance objectives."

FIFPRO's report is asking FIFA to set a so-called floor for the women's game so that minimum standards in key areas such as contracts, pensions and health can be enforced. Perhaps inspiration can be taken from the labor deal the WNBA agreed in 2026. It was long-negotiated deal that ultimately sent a message to female athletes everywhere to push for better pay, conditions and a greater share of the revenue they help generate.

"It is positive that average salaries are increasing for some players and that more are earning a satisfactory wage, but it’s important to note that there is a huge disparity in pay across regions," said Culvin.

"There is also an imbalance in conditions, not only across the globe but also within regions; in Europe, for example, the difference in standards between the east and west is enormous. This is a gulf we need to work hard to narrow; the growth in the most advanced markets must not be completely isolated from the rest of the industry.

With high hopes for the 2027 World Cup in Brazil and recent moves to increase professional football domestically, Germany is aiming to become an example for structural improvement in women's football. Hosting the Euros in 2029 certainly gives them an incentive to improve standards.

While salaries are in the upper tier — in the 2023-24 season, a women's Bundesliga player earned an average base salary of around €48,000 per year — the process of structural development in the country is still in its infancy. A new German football association rule shows that even basic professional structures are still being established. Only since the 2025–26 season have teams in the Women's Bundesliga been required to employ assistant coaches, goalkeeper coaches and athletic coaches on a full-time, professional basis.

"The facilities and the staff members," Nicole Anyomi told DW, were a factor in her making a recent move to London City Lionesses. "We have 30-plus staff members here whereas in Frankfurt we had like seven or eight. You can learn from each person and there is something new to learn every day. I think that's how you develop as a player faster."

Ultimately, the faster the game grows, the greater need to close the gaps.

"Despite playing on different continents, players are connected by their precarity," Culvin said. "The redistribution systems in women's football need to be more effective, touching more players and supporting a more sustainable ecosystem."

Jack Grealish has been left out of Everton’s squad again following an internal disciplinary breach as the Toffees face Newcastle in the Premier League.

Grealish was not part of the travelling party to Tyneside for Everton’s second meeting with the Magpies in the space of five days, with David Moyes’ side emerging 3-1 victors when the teams clashed in the Carabao Cup at the Hill Dickinson Stadium on Thursday.

The 31-year-old winger was absent for that match as punishment for skipping Everton training when he was not authorised to do so.

Grealish, who is in his second spell on loan at Everton, had been in contention to return after missing Everton’s defeat to Arsenal on Saturday, which was put down to illness.

Instead, manager David Moyes left him out of the squad altogether, preferring to name two goalkeepers on the bench for the visit of Matthias Jaissle’s side, and he has opted against including him once again Monday night’s trip to St James’ Park.

The club say this is down to the player not being match fit.

Moyes made two changes from the team that beat Newcastle last week, with Tyler Dibling and Hayden Hackney - who bagged a goal and an assist - dropping to the bench. Jarrad Branthwaite returns to the side, with Jake O’Brien moving to right-back and Merlin Rohl moving forward, while Harrison Armstrong starts alongside James Garner in midfield.

Grealish, who is in the last season of his contract at Manchester City, rejoined Everton on loan on transfer deadline day and has since made six appearances, failing to score.

#1013. Gianni Infantino’s confidential World Cup sell-off documents to be shared with Fifa members

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Infantino’s Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) proposal was rejected by three continental confederations

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Confidential documents linked to Gianni Infantino’s hugely controversial World Cup private investor plan will be made available for members of the Fifa Council to view.

Infantino had sought to set up a company, Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE), to run the commercial interests of the World Cup and its other competitions, with private investors holding a minority stake.

The plan was abandoned in August after three continental confederations rejected it and Uefa threatened a boycott of Fifa competitions.

A letter sent by Uefa on behalf of European members of the Fifa Council on 19 October demanded answers to a series of questions about FFE and a range of other concerns about Infantino’s presidency by Monday.

It’s understood Fifa secretary general Mattias Grafstrom wrote to all Council members on Monday inviting them to view key documents related to the FFE proposal.

Council members – including Fifa vice-presidents such as Uefa president Aleksander Ceferin – have been invited to register their interest within the next two weeks should they wish to view the documents, in person and under specific conditions, at Fifa’s headquarters in Zurich.

The conditions specified are understood to have been applied in order to preserve Fifa’s confidentiality obligations.

For now it is understood the documents to be made available relate solely to FFE. The 19 October letter sought clarity around the Folarin Balogun disciplinary case and a range of other matters, but it is understood a wider response will come to Council members in due course.

Fifa is understood to have viewed Uefa’s two-week deadline to respond to all the 42 areas covered in the letter as unfeasible.

Fifa has been focused on the organisation of the inaugural Under-15 World Cup in Azerbaijan, featuring 189 nations and 3,000 players. It is also preparing for an extraordinary Fifa Congress on 23 November to appoint the hosts for the 2031 and 2035 Women’s World Cups.

Uefa’s ongoing legal action in the United States – where it has sought disclosure of documents linked to FFE – is also understood to have created legal boundaries.

The 19 October letter posed questions around the decision to award exclusivity to Thrive Capital to lead the FFE private investor group. Thrive was founded by Joshua Kushner, the brother of United States President Donald Trump’s son-in-law.

It also sought answers around the timeline surrounding the plan’s development, the $20bn (£15bn) valuation placed on the company, why Fifa felt it was necessary to seek private investment given its healthy cash reserves and whether Infantino stood to gain personally from the plan.

Council members had attended a meeting of the Fifa Council on 15 October and asked Infantino questions in person. One of those members, Football Association chair and Fifa vice-president Debbie Hewitt, said after the meeting that Council members were asked to submit questions in writing.

The Fifa Council is not due to meet again until 16 December. Uefa has pledged to identify a credible alternative candidate to stand against Infantino in the Fifa presidential election next March.

The deadline for candidacy submissions is 18 November.

#1011. WSL talking points: Russo to Arsenal’s rescue and Olid makes Manchester United progress

Gunners edged north London derby while new United manager put the brakes on Manchester City’s winning start

The penalty that allowed Arsenal to come from a goal behind to take the lead may have come with a healthy helping of luck, with the ball having come off Ella Morris’s raised arm as her teammate attempted to clear it, but it could prove to be the turning point Arsenal needed. “It’s been tough. We haven’t got the results we wanted,” penalty scorer Alessia Russo told the BBC afterwards. “This was an important win as far as north London derbies goes. It was really important and this was a great opportunity to try and turn it around.” It has taken seven games for the Gunners to secure their second league win of the season despite high hopes ahead of the new campaign and, while the result was a significant one, there is still a long way to go if Arsenal are to salvage anything from the most disappointing of starts. The performance against Tottenham was far from perfect and, in the first half in particular, sloppy and lacking fight. Tightening up their passing and harnessing the grit they found as they clung onto their lead towards the end of the match will be critical if they are to really kick on from this result. Suzanne Wrack

Is Freya Godfrey England’s future? That’s what Alexia Putellas thinks of her London City Lionesses teammate, and the Spain icon heaped praise on the 21-year-old winger after she scored in her second consecutive WSL game. Godfrey – who made her senior England debut earlier this month against Greece – capitalised on a Khiara Keating mistake to score in the 2-2 draw with Liverpool on Sunday and her all-round display delighted Putellas, who told Sky Sports: “She can arrive where she really wants. I always tell her, she’s a star girl. She will be the future of this club. She has to keep working like she is doing now. She will be the future of England as well as the present.” TG

Manchester United’s display in Sunday’s derby draw was night and day compared to their most recent previous home league fixture against a title challenger, when they were torn apart in a 5-0 defeat at home against Chelsea just six weeks ago. Against Manchester City on Sunday they competed toe-to-toe with the defending champions, and while it would be wrong to suggest that Eva Olid’s team are anywhere near the finished article, their improvements are striking, both with and without the ball. Olid feels that heavy defeat early in her tenure actually helped her side. “It was a hard week after Chelsea but sometimes you need a difficult moment to happen, to react and see exactly where the problems [were] or the things we had to solve as a team,” she said. “It had to happen to now be the team we are.” Tom Garry

Match report: Manchester United 1-1 Manchester City

Birmingham’s first win of the WSL season came in the first encounter between league newcomers this season. Following an impressive point at the Emirates the week before,the 1-0 win over Charlton marked another key step as Amy Merricks’ side continue to settle into the top flight. The Blues were almost made to pay for their profligacy in front of goal against a familiar foe from last season in WSL2. They dominated proceedings and created 20 chances in total but registered just five on target. Océane Hurtré and Lisa Naalsund rattled the crossbar while Lily Crosthwaite missed three gilt-edged opportunities before Wilma Leidhammar struck a 68th minute-winner. “That was the most important thing today,” Merricks said. “We needed to pick up three points and we delivered that. I don’t think the performance was our finest. You could feel the caginess across the pitch and that is something we need to work on. We are in a better place, and we keep pushing.” Sophie Downey

No topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s football

For 51 minutes on Sunday afternoon, it felt like it might just be one of those days for Chelsea. Despite dominating the first half – they created 12 opportunities to Crystal Palace’s four and registered 20 touches in the opposition box – they found themselves trailing and running out of ideas. A key difference between the two sides, however, is the strength in depth available to their respective managers. In bringing on Erin Cuthbert and Sandy Baltimore at half-time, Sonia Bompastor was able to call on the services of two experienced internationals. Cuthbert added a crucial bite to the midfield that had been lacking in the first half while Baltimore set up Melvine Malard to put the Blues in front before scoring from the spot to confirm the three points. In contrast, Jo Potter made just three substitutions with the first coming in the 77th minute. It is this ability to change things from the bench that truly illustrates the gap in class between the eight-time WSL champions and the league newcomers. SD

Brian Sørensen and his Aston Villa side came away with a 3-2 win against Everton. Sørensen, who took over from Natalia Arroyo last month, faced the Merseyside club for the first time since his Goodison Park exit in February. Villa dominated the clash and went 3-0 up within 50 minutes thanks to goals from Noelle Maritz and Amalie Vangsgaard, but they were given a scare following a late comeback push with Holly McNamara and Noémie Mouchon both scoring. Villa saw the game out to take three points – just. Nevertheless, Sørensen will be thrilled with the outcome, especially as it moved his team up to eighth. It also marked the first time since the 2024-25 campaign that Villa have won back-to-back games. “I’m happy, it was overall a good performance,” the interim head coach said. “Of course, maybe they got a bit too excited at the end but I also think we had the opportunities to kill the game off a lot sooner. But three points is three points, that’s all that matters.” Emillia Hawkins

Maisie Symonds’ stunning strike set Brighton on course for a 3-0 victory over West Ham. The Brighton captain broke the deadlock in the 29th minute, meeting a headed clearance with a first-time strike from distance that swerved beyond West Ham goalkeeper Constance Picaud-Inconnu and kissed the post on its way in. It was her second goal of the season, rewarding Brighton’s early dominance. Fran Kirby doubled the lead in the 63rd minute before Kiko Seike struck three minutes later. Brighton’s head coach, Arturo Ruiz, called it his side’s “most complete” performance of the season, praising their confidence and tactical adaptability. Symonds said Brighton “got control” in the second half. It was the Seagulls’ first Women’s Super League clean sheet of the campaign. Mitul Samji

#1010. Harry Kane gives major update on his Bayern Munich future after Ballon d'Or triumph

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Harry Kane’s current contract is due to expire next summer

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Harry Kane expects to sign a new contract with Bayern Munich “within the next few days” after winning the Ballon d’Or last week

The 33-year-old’s current contract is due to expire next summer after he signed a four-year deal when leaving Tottenham in 2023.

There has been speculation over Kane’s future, with some wondering whether he could be tempted back to the Premier League to try to chase down Alan Shearer’s all-time goalscoring record.

However, the England captain is now ready to extend his stay at the Allianz Arena.

“I would say it is more (a matter of) days,” Kane said at a press conference ahead of Tuesday's Champions League match at Atletico Madrid.

"There has been good conversations over this weekend and today as well. I know I keep saying we are close, but we are extremely close now. Details are just details in every contract.

"A lot of the bigger stuff has been ironed out and we are happy with, but in every contract there is loads of little things that go into it, small details that in the end the lawyers have to thrash out and figure out.

“So all in all I would say it is more days than weeks. From what I have heard, the conversations have gone well again today and hopefully we will be in a place to do something within the next few days.”

Last season, Kane scored 73 goals for club and country, while he also won two trophies in Germany and led England to third place at the World Cup.

This ensured that he won the Ballon d’Or, as he became the first Englishman to claim the coveted award since Michael Owen in 2001.

Kane paraded the Ballon d’Or on Saturday, but then missed a second-half penalty and hit the post, as Bayern Munich drew 2-2 with rivals Borussia Dortmund in the Bundesliga in his first match since last Monday’s award ceremony.

“Hi everyone, I just wanted to say I’m extremely proud to be a FC Bayern Munich player,” Kane told the crowd prior to the game. “The support you have shown me since I arrived has been incredible.”

#1009. Matthias Jaissle is stuck in a dangerous tactical limbo, and Newcastle United are in for an extremely bumpy ride

What the new Newcastle manager wants to do vs what is actually happening on the pitch are miles apart, with patience wearing thin among fans

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Matthias Jaissle’s tactical philosophy sounds great on paper, but it’s failing on grass. Shaped by his formative years under Ralf Rangnick at Hoffenheim, then refined in Austria managing FC Liefering and Red Bull Salzburg, and adapted to the idiosyncrasies of Saudi Arabian football with Al-Ahli. He won six trophies with the latter two clubs across five seasons.

At its core, his approach is aggressive, vertical football which places emphasis on the middle of the pitch. Rather than pressing opponents in horizontal banks, Jaissle likes his teams to stay narrow and tempt goalkeepers and defenders to play risky passes.

The instant his team cede possession, he wants the nearest players to swarm the carrier in a compact ‘cage’ where the ball can be won back in around eight seconds, an idea influenced by Rangnick.

His fullbacks and central midfielders stay high when attacking, ensuring that defensive transitions happen 40–50 yards away from their own goal. But if they go wrong, as we saw at Everton on Thursday night, it leaves them open at the back. Very open. The likes of Leeds, Coventry and Everton have proved it’s possible to break through Newcastle in as few as two fairly simple passes. One of those vs Everton came from Jordan Pickford.

At present, Jaissle’s Newcastle are a dream to play against. They fly out of the traps, create chances (which they tend not to take), then hit a lull. Opponents already have a blueprint to beat them: rope-a-dope until the lactic hits, and then pounce in the acres of space that emerge in the Newcastle half. After 23 minutes on Thursday night, Jacob Ramsey diligently followed his manager's instructions and counter-pressed into Everton’s far corner; Fabian Schar stepped out of defence to cover the midfielder, leaving Burn one-on-one with Thierno Barry high up the pitch. Everton don’t find the pass, but it’s a warning of how vulnerable Newcastle are.

Soon after, Hayden Hackney dropped into the back line to get on the ball and, in accordance with Jaissle’s tactics, Nico Gonzalez tracks him, leaving Ramsey to man the entire middle of the pitch alone.

Later, young winger Tyler Dibbling finds himself inside a Jaissle pressing ‘cage’ surrounded by four Newcastle players, but finds a pass to Merlin Röhl, who breaks into Newcastle’s final third where he makes a poor decision and lets them off the hook. Another warning sign.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

Minutes later, Amar Dedic loses possession at right back. A tiring Nico Gonzalez is late to press, then a tiring Jacob Ramsey is late to the press, and James Gardner strokes home to the delight of watching Prime Minister Andy Burnham.

Jaissle’s successful teams have had young, hungry, hyper-athletic players built for 90 minutes of non-stop sprinting; not many in Newcastle’s current squad fit that mould, and they look vulnerable at the end of halves.

On 45 minutes, Jacob Ramsey commits a foul; the ref plays a good advantage, then doesn’t have the legs to track Hayden Hackney, who scores. Ramsey didn’t reemerge for the second half.

Out of possession, Newcastle have absolutely zero control, but on it they are quite exciting. The idea is direct penetration; they rarely indulge in slow, horseshoe passing around the back. The objective is to break lines as quickly as possible and turn possession into a shot within seconds. They had 28 to Everton’s 11 in this game.

Jaissle has to somehow make Newcastle more solid in midfield, and offer the centre backs and goalkeeper more protection. Switching from two in midfield to three could help, but he doesn’t strike me as a man to row back on his principles after a dozen games.

After 69 minutes, the game is over when Thierno Barry applies a neat finish to a Kiernan Dewsbury-Hall cross.

Newcastle have never felt in control and on top in a game for more than 30 minutes this season, which is an obvious concern. Nearly 8,000 Newcastle fans travelled to Merseyside to watch the team be carved open. Rarely has an away end emptied as fast, with less than 10% hanging around to clap/boo.

David Moyes wasn’t exactly gushing in his post-match press conference, aware that Newcastle dominated for the first 15-20 minutes of the game and Everton had to weather that storm: “I thought it was a tough game, and we got the goals at good times”.

Jaissle said, “It’s a bit shocking at the moment, because overall the game was not that bad. It’s a bit of the story of the season so far that in a situation where it really counts we lack the clinical approach to solve the situations.”

He can be quite robotic in his press conferences, which will do nothing for his approval rating on Tyneside. “It’s a learning process, but you don’t get the time. Especially with these young lads.”

Speak to anyone behind the scenes at the club, and they will reiterate that Jaissle is a long-term bet for the owners. Unless scorelines get seriously ugly, he will be given time to apply his methods.

Pointing to this game’s statistics (Newcastle had an xG of 2.14 vs Everton’s 1.67, 9 shots on target to their 5 and 38 touches in the box to their 19) hints at a flickering light in the tunnel of disappointing results. But the we’re-not-taking-our-chances defence will only work for so long. Managers whose players consistently don’t take their chances tend to lose their jobs.

A former goalkeeper, Ketch joined FourFourTwo as Deputy Editor in 2022 having worked across ChronicleLive, LeedsLive, Hull Daily Mail, YorkshireLive, Teesside Gazette and the Huddersfield Examiner as a Northern Football Editor. Prior to that he was the Senior Writer at BBC Match of the Day magazine. He has interviewed the likes of Harry Kane, Trent Alexander-Arnold, Gareth Southgate and attended two World Cup finals and two Champions League finals. He has been a Newcastle United season ticket holder since 2000 and has a deep knowledge on the history and culture of football shirts.

#1008. Premier League: 10 talking points from the weekend’s action

Bournemouth’s transfer nous puts United to shame, Araújo is winning admirers at Anfield and Suzuki adapts swiftly at Villa

The three Bournemouth goalscorers cost a combined £85m, joining from Vasco da Gama, Middlesbrough, and Porto. The Cherries are smart at investing, far more so than Manchester United, who have wasted a lot of money by failing to look outside the box for players like Rayan, Marcus Tavernier and Evanilson. United may not have the wealth they previously showed in the transfer market but Bournemouth are showing what can be done within a budget and, more importantly, will be able to make a profit on signings. United, however, only know losses as everyone’s price tag diminishes the moment they come through the Old Trafford door. Jason Wilcox and others can point to certain factors that are against them but there are quality signings to be made at the right price if you have the ability to find them. Will Unwin

Match report: Manchester United 0-3 Bournemouth

Will Unwin: Carrick left carrying can for institutional failings

Aston Villa were quite happy to sell Emiliano Martínez but many feared it would be difficult to find an upgrade on the World Cup-winning goalkeeper. They have seemingly done so in the form of the £30m signing Zion Suzuki, who was superb against Manchester City. Nicolas Jackson’s goals stole the headlines but Suzuki’s bounty of saves ensured that Villa were victorious, while also impressing with his distribution. ”He’s ambitious. I think it’s very important, his mentality,” Unai Emery said. “Of course, we need a keeper first to save us in the goal, but as well we need one keeper to try to help us in our buildup. And in buildup, he’s a really fantastic player because he can play short, he can understand where is the superiority to break the opponent’s press. He has qualities to do long ball, getting our players in attack. So, we are very, very impressed how he adapted so quick with us.” WU

Match report: Aston Villa 2-1 Manchester City

Aside from the reaction to the half-time and full-time scores from Old Trafford, the biggest noise at Anfield was generated by Ronald Araújo showing no mercy in his challenges on Malick Yalcouyé and Charalampos Kostoulas. The on-loan Barcelona defender immediately endeared himself to the Kop with his commitment and quality, and was again in commanding form to help Andoni Iraola record his first Premier League home win as Liverpool head coach. “I think we all enjoyed watching Ronald fighting,” said Iraola. “He’s very good in the duels. Even the first goal, he wins two duels in a row and defensively he’s been really, really good. I’m happy for him because I’ve taken him out in the last two games because we needed more offensive things. But he has continued working with no issues and today we needed him more. He has given a very, very good 90 minutes.” Andy Hunter

João Pedro is unlikely to make a swift return after picking up an injury in training. The Chelsea striker missed the defeat to Tottenham and had a scan on Sunday. Xabi Alonso did not sound optimistic after the Spurs game. The expectation is João Pedro will miss this week’s games against Liverpool and Manchester United as a minimum, leaving Alonso with problems in attack. It was strange he did not start Danny Welbeck against Spurs. Chelsea had no focal point and there are questions over their depth. Emmanuel Emegha, another struggling with injury, is yet to play since joining from Strasbourg. It is fair to wonder if selling Nicolas Jackson to Villa was the right move. Chelsea have played two league games without João Pedro this season and have lost both without scoring a goal. Cole Palmer and Morgan Rogers are not as effective without him. Jacob Steinberg

Barney Ronay: Glitch in Chelsea’s coding costs Alonso while resurgent Spurs are all systems go

Mikel Arteta says he has been compiling a dossier of evidence of other managers straying outside the technical area after the Arsenal manager was shown a yellow card during the 2-0 win over Everton. It was his second of the season and leaves the Spaniard at risk of suspension if he gets one more, although Arteta suggested he is by no means the worst offender. “There are managers who have the record in the league, 36 times in 10 minutes [they] leave the touchline – no yellows,” he said, naming no names. “I am clipping all of that so I now have a massive storage of images, so if somebody comes to me I can say: ‘I am not in the record yet.’ Somebody else has the record so let’s see. Then it’s 36 yellow cards in 10 minutes for the managers. I don’t know what we are going to do – let’s see.” Ed Aarons

Nico González cost Manchester City £50m when they signed him early in 2025, as part of that January spree as Pep Guardiola tried to arrest the first real slump of his Premier League career. Although he started nine league games that season and 17 last, González made very little impact at the Etihad. He probably wasn’t even the best Nico González in world football, given the Argentinian winger’s performances for Juventus and Atlético. But the Spanish Nico González clearly is a player of substance, his calm in midfield one of the few undoubted positives for Newcastle so far this season. Only Lewis Hall has made more tackles per game than him, he set up Sven Botman’s goal at Coventry, while he’s made more key passes per game than anybody other than Harvey Barnes. At £48m, he may end up representing extremely good value. Jonathan Wilson

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

Match report: Crystal Palace 0-2 Newcastle

To ask a question that might be a segment on the Football Cliches podcast, is there a more “swirling litter” venue in the Premier League than the Stadium of Light? At this point it should be obvious this was not a classic. In part that is down the conditions – long balls ran away from players on both sides with frequency, and crisp packets were the only thing to trouble the nets at either end. Managing the Europa League was always going to be a challenge for Sunderland and returning from a midweek trip to Poland to earn a point against a team who have had a week to prepare is a good result, even if the Black Cats finish the weekend at the foot of the table. Tom Bassam

In spectacular style, Oscar Bobb’s wait for a first Premier League goal for Fulham came to an end at Coventry. Bobb was signed in January, fitting the recruitment template that brought success and stability under Marco Silva, a manager adept at regenerating talent. Social media footage from the away end showed Fulham fans ask what Bobb, weaving and bobbing, was doing only for him to feint past two Coventry defenders and score. That broke the deadlock when Coventry appeared fully capable of claiming a point or better. It remains to be seen whether Álvaro Arbeloa possesses the some restorative powers as Silva. After two wins in succession, two clean sheets and a first win away from Craven Cottage since February, early-season panic has dissipated. For now. If survival is Fulham’s first objective, then successive wins over the promoted teams Hull and Coventry were minimum requirements. Though should Fulham aim much higher? Silva departed because his ambitions were not met. John Brewin

Brentford are still yet to win away from home in the league but are also unbeaten on their travels. The draws at Leeds, Bournemouth and Aston Villa can be considered decent results, but this goes in the missed opportunity pile. So far Hull have presented a stiffer challenge at MKM Stadium than predicted, but in terms of expectations for Brentford this fixture has more in common with playing Sunderland at home than it does with their previous draws on the road. Against Sunderland and at Hull, Keith Andrews’ side struggled when the onus was on the them to make the game. The Bees play like they would rather not have the ball. In this one, they had plenty of shots – 14 in total – but only Dango Ouattara and belatedly Jaidon Anthony truly troubled Konstantinos Tzolakis. Brentford need Igor Thiago firing again. TB

With Nottingham Forest the Premier League’s joint-lowest scorers, the pressure on Liam Delap is increasing. At Ipswich, where he was a rare bright spot with 12 goals in the relegation season of 2024-25, Delap was booed on every touch. The jeers got louder when each of his four attempts on goal missed their target. Only three of 18 Premier League shots in a Forest shirt have been on target. The raw materials that Chelsea moved for in summer 2025 remain present, the physical prowess and ability to find promising positions. The finishing touches are, at present, lacking, when Forest need someone to start scoring. Failing to take their chances at Portman Road left Forest in the relegation zone, endangering Oliver Glasner, when the ownership is trigger-happy with managers. Chris Wood, previously Forest’s talisman, came on in the 89th minute for Delap, but has been no super-sub so far, without a goal or assist from seven cameo league appearances. JB

Match report: Ipswich 1-1 Nottingham Forest

#1007. Daily briefing: The three red flags of suspicious journals

Hello Nature readers, would you like to get this Briefing in your inbox free every day? Sign up here.

By the time a baby is born, its brain has lost large numbers of neurons with genetic abnormalities.Credit: Getty

Around the time of birth, the developing human brain mysteriously clears out a vast number of mutation-riddled neurons. Researchers found that more than one-quarter of neurons sampled from human fetuses had some kind of chromosomal abnormality, but this percentage plummeted to 6% in the brains of babies who’d just been born. The findings reveal a new mechanism for regulating how many neurons a person has and for deciding which fetal neurons are allowed to persist in the brain, says paediatric neurogeneticist and study co-author Diane Shao.

A new report suggests that it might be possible to launch a swarm of satellites that reflect sunlight away from the planet to cool the global temperatures in as few as 20-40 years. The timeline of such a ‘planetary sunshade’ would depend on the rate at which heavy-lift rockets that could carry the materials into deep space are developed, the report says. A lot of people think this idea is “just fantasy”, says space-systems engineer Chantal Cappelletti. But the falling cost of space launches has made the prospect of space-based solar geoengineering seem more realistic.

Reference: Planetary Sunshade Institute report

Researchers have identified three warning signs that suggest journals might be engaging in suspicious publishing activities. These red flags are, for any given journal in a single year: a doubling of publication output; having more than 70% of published articles originating from a single country; and having at least 15% of articles flagged by the Problematic Paper Screener, a free online tool. Using titles on the database OpenAlex, the team identified 3,753 journals that met at least one of these criteria. These signals can help to identify journals that merit further investigation — but do not prove that titles are problematic, say the study authors.

Reference: Zenodo preprint (not peer reviewed)

The results of a trial that intentionally infected volunteers with a weakened strain of dengue virus hint at why the disease hits harder in people who are infected for a second time — an issue that has stymied the development of a dengue vaccine. Researchers found that people who’d had dengue before tended to have higher viral loads and more hyperinflammatory signals on second exposure than did people who had never had the virus. The people with the highest viral load had fewer antibodies to fight infection, and these antibodies were less effective.

Reference: Science Translational Medicine paper

To better understand how individuals might respond to certain treatments, researchers should work to develop the ‘immunome’: a comprehensive characterization of immune health across cells, tissues, organs and molecular interactions, argues a group of medical researchers. To start, scientists should identify key measures that could be used to flag any immune features that are weakened or declining. “If scientists can work out which measurements matter, validate them across diverse populations and establish when acting on them improves disease outcomes, immune health could become a routine dimension of medicine,” the group writes.

Ecologist Sage Raymond, who has previously been homeless, studies the interactions between urban wildlife and people living unsheltered. On a draft of her previous work, a reviewer commented that she and her colleagues seemed “naive about homelessness”. “That assumption shook me: it suggested someone with my history did not belong in academia,” Raymond writes. Her past has equipped her with skills that enable her research, but “many of the life experiences that bring diversity to science are invisible,” which leaves room for harmful assumptions, she writes.

Ashley Kurpiel took part in a clinical trial of the drug garetosmab, a treatment for fibrodysplasia ossificans progressiva (FOP) — an extremely rare disorder in which connective tissue gradually turns into bone. The drug can’t reverse Kurpiel’s disease progression, but her participation can still provide researchers with valuable safety and efficacy data. (The New York Times | 6 min read)

doi: https://doi.org/10.1038/d41586-026-03548-4

Today I’m pondering life’s important questions, such as: which animals could I beat in a running race? The answer is more complicated than you might think, say researchers. Many creatures have a higher top speed than the average person, but accelerate more slowly, researchers say. Distance is another factor, as speedy animals might not have the endurance to reach the finish line.

Unfortunately, I lack both speed and endurance, so my chances of a win are generally slim.

Let me know which animals you think you could best, along with any feedback on this newsletter, at briefing@nature.com.

Jacob Smith, associate editor, Nature Briefing

#1006. Everton beat Newcastle again as 10-man Magpies booed off by own fans after dismal display

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Newcastle 0-1 Everton: The Magpies slipped to their second defeat against Everton in the space of four days

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Everton returned to winning ways in the Premier League as Thierno Barry's second-half goal secured a 1-0 victory against Newcastle at St James' Park.

Following a first half with few clear opportunities, the decisive moment arrived shortly after the restart when Barry poked home his fourth league goal of the campaign.

A frustrating evening for Newcastle worsened in the closing minutes when substitute Jacob Ramsey was shown two quick yellow cards, leaving the hosts with 10 men as they slipped to 13th in the Premier League table. The Magpies were booed off at half time and full time, piling the pressure on manager Matthias Jaissle.

The match took place four days after Everton's 3-1 win over Newcastle in the Carabao Cup fourth round. Both sides made two changes to their line-ups, with Anthony Elanga and Joelinton starting for the Magpies, while Jarrad Branthwaite and Harrison Armstrong came in for the visitors.

Harvey Barnes looked lively on Newcastle's left, curling a shot wide before a looping cross drifted past the far post. Everton goalkeeper Jordan Pickford was then required to collect Will Osula's deflected cross from a tight angle.

Joelinton had an effort blocked by James Tarkowski and Merlin Rohl fired over as both teams sought a breakthrough. James Garner blasted a free-kick into the Newcastle wall, before Barnes forced Pickford to tip the ball over after his cross struck Branthwaite.

Joelinton shot wide from distance before Everton created late first-half chances, with Jake O'Brien failing to head in Kiernan Dewsbury-Hall's cross and Harrison Armstrong skewing a shot wide.

The Toffees took the lead four minutes after the interval. A clever pass from a free-kick set Tyrique George free on the left to shoot low at Lukas Hornicek. The ball squeezed under the goalkeeper, allowing Barry to tap in the loose ball after a VAR check for two tight offsides.

Hornicek saved Branthwaite's header as Everton sought a second, while Fabian Schar shot over and Pickford held Joe Willock's header. Hornicek then denied Dewsbury-Hall and saved O'Brien's effort from the resulting corner.

Barnes' cross was almost converted by Elanga, but his shot hit the post and rolled along the line before being cleared. Pickford later punched away a Jacob Murphy corner before Ramsey volleyed wide, with the goalkeeper subsequently denying Yoane Wissa twice.

In eight minutes of added time, Ramsey received his marching orders after picking up two yellow cards in quick succession, concluding a disappointing night for the home side as Everton claimed all three points.

#1004. Trump's diesel deal with Russia is unlikely to significantly lower global fuel prices despite expectations of rapid relief

As the world's largest diesel exporter, the US benefits from high prices. At home, however, consumers are feeling the strain of rising living costs. Why Donald Trump's deal with Russia is unlikely to change that.

With or without a deal with Russia, diesel prices on global markets are unlikely to fall significantly anytime soon.

That is the assessment of experts interviewed by DW regarding the latest fuel-supply agreement between US President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin.

"The main reason for high diesel prices is the war in Iran and the simultaneous disruption of shipping through the Strait of Hormuz and the Bab al-Mandeb Strait," said Samina Sultan, a foreign trade expert at the German Economic Institute (IW) in Cologne.

The situation has led to production outages and made fuel shipments "more expensive, less secure and more difficult," she said.

Trump's deal with Russia also has an additional geopolitical dimension, Sultan said: "It causes the wars in Ukraine and Iran to become completely intertwined."

Things are looking up, though. Roughly 13.5 million barrels of crude oil are once again flowing through the Strait of Hormuz a day, according to shipping and commodities analytics firm Kpler.

But for refined products such as diesel, volumes remain far lower at around 677,000 barrels per day, compared with 3.6 million barrels before the war.

Carsten Fritsch, a commodities analyst at Commerzbank, also attributes the price increases to the wars.

"If nothing changes in Ukraine and the Middle East, I see very few ways to resolve these supply bottlenecks," he said.

In a social media post on October 9, Trump announced that he would temporarily suspend some sanctions on Russia and begin importing Russian diesel.

He wrote "diesel prices for Americans and, indeed, the world, will be COMING DOWN, IN RECORD NUMBERS, AND FAST!" in a mix of lowercase and all caps.

Russia confirmed the arrangement. Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told Russian state news agency TASS on October 13 that supplying diesel fuel was "in the interests of Russia, the United States and global energy markets."

Diesel prices in the US and many EU countries have risen sharply over the past 12 months.

According to the US Energy Information Administration (EIA), prices in the US have climbed by about 60% and now stand at $6.30 per gallon, equivalent to $1.66 (or €1.49) per liter of diesel.

But even if Russia were able to flood global markets with cheap diesel, prices would not fall nearly as much as they recently rose, something all of the experts contacted by DW agree on.

Many refineries around the Gulf region have suffered disruptions or damage, while transporting fuel via shadow fleets and securing insurance remains costly, cumbersome and risky.

Another key shift is that Russia is no longer the world's largest diesel exporter. In fact, it is facing its own fuel shortages at home.

The US is now the world's biggest diesel exporter. In 2025, it exported an average of 1.26 million barrels of diesel per day, accounting for roughly 15.4% of global diesel exports.

At the same time, Russia fell to second place with a 9.5% share, and that was before major Ukrainian drone attacks on its refineries.

Besides the new US-Russia diesel agreement, Trump also recently floated the idea of US diesel export restrictions. But the idea was abandoned because it could lead to even higher diesel prices in the country, according to Samina Sultan.

"There simply is not enough diesel storage capacity in the United States," Sultan said. "Production would have to be reduced, and then prices would rise again."

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

If the US were to impose export restrictions on diesel, buyers in Latin America and the European Union would be hit particularly hard. Since Russia invaded Ukraine, EU countries have increasingly imported diesel from the US instead of Russia because of sanctions.

"An export ban merely redistributes the shortage; it does not solve it," said ING chief economist Carsten Brzeski.

"Global prices would continue to rise, while refineries would scale back production as margins shrink," he added.

Export restrictions aside, few people consider that the US-Russia diesel deal will have any big impact.

According to calculations by the platform The World Data, the promised shipment of 2.2 million barrels of diesel from Russia would not even cover a single day's US diesel demand of roughly 4 million barrels.

Even if all of the diesel volumes announced by Trump were combined, totaling 35.8 million barrels, they would only cover about nine days of US domestic demand.

"I CANNOT OVERSTATE HOW MUCH OF A NOTHING BURGER THIS IS," Canadian oil market analyst Rory Johnston wrote in an all-caps post on X shortly after the announcement.

Russia would normally export almost 10 times that volume if its refinery fleet was not being targeted by Ukrainian drone attacks, he added.

Canada also supplies diesel to the United States. Roughly 80% of all US diesel imports come from its northern neighbor.

Given Trump's verbal attacks on Canada and the ongoing trade dispute, analysts view the prospect of Canada supplying significantly more diesel to the US as highly unlikely.

This piece was originally published in German.

#1003. Football Daily | Fleetwood go their own way to down Arsenal and live Carabao Cup dream

Sign up now! Sign up now! Sign up now? Sign up now!

Having made a passing reference to Mick Fleetwood in Tuesday’s thrilling edition of your favourite email, Football Daily genuinely wasn’t expecting to be repeatedly typing that particular F-word in our lead story in today’s edition. While we were aware Arsenal were in the coastal town of Fleetwood for a Fizzy Cup tie that could scarcely have been less glamorous than the previous evening’s Ballon d’Or ceremony at the Palladium, the needle on our patented Potential Shock-o-Meter had barely moved before a match pitting the Premier League champions against a side struggling in League Two. Even with the residual winds from Storm Boelo still buffeting the ground, we presumed Arsenal’s second string would have enough about them to record a comfortable win at Highbury, over 20 years after they left a London stadium of the same name to begin their residency at the Emirates. It was not to be and almost five months to the day since exiting a cup competition on penalties following a curiously flat and uninspired display, Mikel Arteta’s side exited a cup competition on penalties following etc, and so on.

Considering their team came into this game on the back of consecutive defeats by Cheltenham and Exeter, Fleetwood’s Cod Army would almost certainly have settled for seeing their players avoid embarrassment but after watching them go ahead against a team of Fancy Dans who were visibly labouring in the miserable conditions expectations were duly raised. Arsenal equalised courtesy of a scrambled Viktor Gyökeres effort that is unlikely to trouble the Puskas Award jury, before all hell broke loose when young Max Dowman was sent off for retaliation following a Harrison Neal challenge that – depending entirely on what team you support – was a potential career-ender or wasn’t even a foul. While he is not yet old enough to drive, get a tattoo or vote, Dowman has apparently been around long enough to earn himself a stinging rebuke from his manager, who conveyed the impression the 16-year-old could look forward to being sent to bed without any supper and having his screen-time vastly reduced.

A penalty shootout in which yet another Brazilian missed a crucial spot-kick for the Gunners ended in victory for Fleetwood, when Conor Haughey fired past Illan Meslier to make it five successful kicks out of five for the hosts. The second teenager to disgrace himself on the night, the young man from Norn Iron proceeded to drop a different kind of F-bomb in a post-match interview with Sky Sports. Asked what had been going through his mind before he took his penalty, Haughey replied: “Hit the top corner and run like f**k.”

Despite the post-watershed lateness of the hour, Sky’s pitchside reporter felt compelled to apologise to viewers for the youngster’s forthright response. While Arteta is left to focus on making sure his players get their act together ahead of Sunday’s trip to Liverpool, Fleetwood head coach, Matt Lawlor, can look forward to tonight’s quarter-final draw. “I’ve got no preference whatsoever,” he said. “We’ve got a big game at home [against Bristol Rovers] on Saturday and I want to win it. I would absolutely love to make an amazing night into an amazing week.” For Arsenal, on a night when heroes were hard to find, the dream of a domestic treble went its own way.

The MBM OGs are in tandem tonight for steaming hot live action. Join Scott Murray from 8pm GMT for Carling Cup fourth-round updates from Liverpool 3-2 Chelsea  while Rob Smyth will be on deck at the same time to talk us through Arsenal 1-1 Benfica in the Women’s Champions League.

“Our club holds deep respect for China, its history, its culture, and its citizens, as well as for the millions of Chinese fans who feel affection and admiration for Real Madrid. The club joins the public apology expressed by Kylian Mbappé, in which the player himself has conveyed his regret for his words and reiterated his respect for the Chinese people” – Real Madrid are in crisis PR mode as Mbappé’s Chairman Mao comments reach the second day of saying sorry.

double quotation markYour headline Mbappé’s China Crisis leads me to point out he was born in Paris and is not one half of a synth pop duo from Kirkby, Merseyside – Kev The Poet, Tiverton (born in Kirkby).

double quotation markSo pathetic Arsenal get knocked out of the Carabao Cup by plucky Fleetwood Town. I think that Michael Carrick should be sacked immediately! – Nigel Sanders.

double quotation markThe Nevada in Florida story reminded me of my coaching time with under-11s in Maryland in the 90s. The rule from the league was clear, if you’re leading by six goals at half-time, take off the star(s) for the second half. Football was designed to develop as well as to win. As for parents, I had them stand in an area I designated where during game-time they could encourage their scions but not encroach. This was unusual but they understood this strange Brit in a faraway land and it worked well for everyone. Happy times and no police needed, except welcomed as parents! – Jeremy Foxon.

double quotation markRegarding the quote of the day from Wayne Rooney in yesterday’s Football Daily, he seems to be inferring that players from Brentford and Wolves are not good enough for Manchester United. This is from a man who signed for said United in the summer of 2004 from Everton, who (checks online encyclopaedia) finished 17th in the Premier League a couple of months earlier. Pot/kettle? – Tracey in Leicester.

If you have any, please send letters to the.boss@theguardian.com. Today’s prizeless letter o’ the day goes to … Kev The Poet. Terms and conditions for our competitions, when we run them, are here.

#1000. Andres Iniesta on his rise to becoming an all-time great
